headline: West end flood at 4.8 knots: bass stack the seam, mackerel push the east end ebb
subhead: The tide swung hard again this week and the Canal answered with its first real fall push — bass, blues, and bait moving together on the current change.
body_markdown:
The 5:40 a.m. ebb at the Railroad Bridge was running better than 4 knots by full swing Thursday, and that's the number that mattered this week. When the west end current gets up over 4, it starts stacking bait against the pilings and the rock edge below the bridge, and this week it finally had something to stack — mackerel, in numbers regulars haven't seen since spring, pushing through with the tide and dragging stripers and a scattered class of bluefish right along with them.

We flagged this last week — said the striper run through the canal was building on the tide changes, a classic early-fall pattern as bass funnel through with the current — and that's exactly what showed up. The difference this week is the bait finally caught up to the fish. Herring and mackerel have started moving through the ditch on both stages of the tide, not just the ebb, and that's turned what was a thin, opportunistic bite into something with real teeth behind it.

East end has been the more consistent read. The rip that forms off the Sandwich side on the last two hours of the east-running ebb has been holding bass in the 28 to 34-inch range, with the better fish coming right at the color change where the clean Bay water meets the darker canal push. Guys working that seam with 2-ounce Deadly Dicks and diamond jigs in mackerel colors — chrome with a green or blue back — have done the most damage, worked with a lift-and-drop through the lower third of the water column where the current is folding the bait against the rock. Bucktails in white and olive, 1.5 to 2 ounces, fished on a slow swing across the seam, have also been picking up fish, especially in the last 45 minutes before dead low when the current starts to soften and the stripers push up out of the deeper slot to feed on the disorganized bait.

West end has been more of a grind, but when it's turned on it's turned on hard. The current seam that sets up off Mashnee Island on the building flood — usually the two hours either side of the 4.8-knot peak — has been the money window. Bass are using that seam the same way they use the east end rip: holding tight to the edge where the fast water meets the slower inside water, letting the current do the work while they pick off mackerel and the last of the summer's peanut bunker getting swept through. Tube and worm trolled slow along that edge has worked, and so has a slow-retrieved swimming plug — a Bomber Long A or similar — cast up-current and let swing through the seam on a semi-slack line.

Blues have been mixed in on both ends, but they're not the story yet. Most of what's showing is in the 3 to 5-pound class, snapping at the same mackerel-pattern jigs and getting caught more as bycatch than as a target. That could change fast — the bigger bluefish push that's been building from Montauk on down the coast hasn't shown its hand in the canal yet, but with bait now funneling through consistently, it's only a matter of time before a heavier class of blues finds the same buffet the bass have found.

What hasn't shown up yet, at least not with any consistency, is albies or bonito. There's chatter of small showings on the Buzzards Bay side outside Phinneys Harbor and around Wings Neck, which tracks with the broader pattern of false albacore and bonito pushing north and west along the warm-water edge this month. If that edge keeps tightening bait against structure the way it has south of here, don't be shocked if a few fish start showing on the west end flats near Mashnee or in the deeper water off Hog Island on calm mornings. Small epoxy jigs and Deadly Dicks in the half-ounce to ¾-ounce range, worked fast on light leader, would be the play if that materializes — but right now it's a maybe, not a bet.

Slack water has been the great equalizer this week, and not in a good way. Both ends go quiet fast once the current drops off — the bite can go from steady action to nothing in the space of twenty minutes as the bait scatters and the fish stop holding position. The trick has been timing arrival to catch the last hour of a stage and the first hour of the next, rather than fishing dead slack itself, which has been close to a waste of time on both ends this week.

Looking ahead, the moon is building toward the next phase and tidal range is going to keep increasing over the next several days, which should push current speeds up on both ends and pull even more bait through the system. That lines up with what's happening from the Cape's south side on down — the fall migration is picking up steam, and the canal is typically one of the last funnels that bait and fish pass through before scattering into the Bay and Sound. If the pattern holds, expect the window to widen — earlier starts on the ebb, later pushes on the flood, and a better class of bass showing as more mackerel and herring get squeezed through the ditch. The next 72 hours should tell whether this was the opening act or just a preview.
